stances_toward.note: The IMF is both lifeline and constraint: the 2023 programme (augmented in June 2025, combined 3rd and 4th reviews, about USD 884m released; about USD 3.64bn disbursed in all) stalled in 2026 when the IMF withheld a tranche of about USD 1.3bn over revenue mobilisation, the exchange rate, banking and subsidies (April 2026), and Dhaka is negotiating a new three-year USD 4.5-5bn package (mission July 2026); in July the IMF endorsed the government's reform agenda. Dhaka needs the money and resists the conditions. Cooling for now; no finalised deal found.

stances_toward.note: Cooperation by necessity that Addis Ababa presents as its own programme: the 48-month Extended Credit Facility (about USD 3.4bn, approved 29 Jul 2024, together with the float of the birr) backs the 'Homegrown Economic Reform Agenda'; the fifth review was completed on 1 Jul 2026 (about USD 464m released, about USD 2.65bn disbursed in all, about USD 200m of it brought forward for the fuel-price shock of the Middle East war), the IMF welcoming the agreement-in-principle with Eurobond holders and asking for fuel subsidies to be phased out and the restructuring completed. Partner rather than reluctant partner: no resistance to the conditions was found in the sources read. The war of 23 Sep 2026 is not in the review text; the sixth review, on end-June 2026 criteria, is the next test. Bond none.

stances_toward.note: The IMF is Lebanon's route back to credit: the 2022 staff-level agreement stalled for lack of reforms; in August 2026 parliament passed the bank resolution law, which the IMF welcomed as a significant step (the president referred one amendment on central-bank independence to the Constitutional Council); Georgieva met Salam on 29 September. A new staff-level agreement still needs the financial gap law, a 2027 budget and a medium-term fiscal framework (and, per the mid-September mission, a VAT rise to 12%). Partner, warming - but conditioned; the government is moving faster than any since 2019. Bond none.
